When naming this post, I realized how hard it is to give a proper description of the vaporwave genra. I'll quote a discussion over at the site-that-shall-not-be-named, as it describes it quite well:

... I think a vaporwave song or album needs to do the following things;

  • Make the user feel an alien feeling, or generally out of body
  • The Music must be contained in "packaging" that also evokes these feelings
  • The Music has some sort of futuristic/dystopian feel, or "world that never was" vibe

-- Darksleep

I think you hit the nail on the head with your bullet points and I agree completely, although the third bullet point is perhaps a little too rigid but still close enough.

My problem with a large portion of vaporwave is that lots of people don't seem to understand, or be aware of, this explanation you have laid out, which is something that has been there since the beginning in some form and is still here today, even if the genre has evolved a lot into new sound territories and pushed this concept perhaps right to the edge and beyond.

Lots of people have different views of what it is, which I think will pop up in this thread. I'll bold them all and explain why I disagree with them:

It's all about 80's/90's childhood nostalgia

I disagree with this one entirely, and it's one of the ones that bugs me the most. I think the reason that 90's tropes occur in vaporwave albums that do understand the overall concept, is because of the whole "past's vision of the future" angle that some vaporwave takes, which then led to people thinking the whole genre was about 80's or 90's nostalgia. And though to create the "out of body" effect you speak of does rely on evoking a strange nostalgia at times, it isn't the start and end point of the genre. When I see pictures of that jazz cup posted on this sub, or clips from 90's kids TV shows, it just drives me crazy with how pointless it makes this place feel. Which leads perfectly onto...

It's an internet based meme music

This is the worst view of vaporwave of all. I think vaporwave, in particular the cover of Floral Shoppe, did spawn a seapunk-inspired form of memey internet art, which you can find just by searching "vaporwave" on Tumblr, but I don't see this as being vaporwave at all. It's just a continuation of the seapunk idea with statues replacing dolphins. This isn't a knock on Floral Shoppe either, but rather a knock on the misinterpretation of vaporwave that has resulted in this new form of seapunk to arise under the vaporwave name.

It's a critique of capitalism through parody of music associated with the corporate world, such as smooth jazz and muzak

While this is perhaps a small part of the genre, it's such a minimal aspect of vaporwave that the genre should not be defined by it. There are only very few artists in this genre who actively try to make a political point with their music, and many of the early artists who have been cited as doing so have all rejected this idea in the past - Vektroid being the most notable example. This idea originally came about from Adam Harper's vaporwave article for Dummy, which was also one of the biggest moments in vaporwave's growth as a genre, so it is easy to see why this concept has been attached to the genre over time. This isn't a knock on Adam Harper either, as an aside, as in general I think his music writing is excellent and that vaporwave article still had some really good points in regardless of this error.

It's just slowed down and chopped up music

This is the one where people want to identify vaporwave purely on a musical standpoint, and they can't seem to understand that the genre has evolved way beyond the original chopped and screwed eccojams approach. In this sense, I don't think vaporwave is actually even a genre at this point, but a full art movement that approaches the concepts Darksleep mentioned in his post, and as such encompasses many different styles of music.

Vaporwave is future funk

I think this one came about with the crossover success of both Saint Pepsi and then later Macross 82-99, who are probably a lot of people's first view of the genre. Saint Pepsi, who was originally a more "chopped and screwed" style of vaporwave artist and an associate of Luxury Elite and Fortune 500, later made Hit Vibes which took off and launched his music career. However, I don't actually view Hit Vibes as a vaporwave album at all, as it shares none of the ideals put forward by Darksleep.

Again, this isn't a knock on Saint Pepsi or future funk music in general, as some of it can be enjoyable, but rather just trying to distinguish a difference between the two.

So overall, I do agree completely with Darksleep here, but I think my only point I would further add is that because it's such an artistic and conceptual genre that even the works that do apply to this ideal he has laid out are so wide ranging it can still be really confusing. For example, I think both mine and Telepath's 2814 album and Vektroid's Floral Shoppe album are both vaporwave under these rules, yet they sound and feel completely different from one another.

Beyond this, my only other point would be to say that once we start applying more rigid rules as to what it should be in an ideological sense, then the experimentation and such would naturally begin to decline, so it's a double edged sword. However, it could be fruitful for people to agree to some really basic outline of sorts, to build from.

My final point I would like to add, is vaporwave has become a "scene", which is now a really large one full of different people with different ideas, which is again another double edged sword.

-- dreamcatalogue (HKE & telepath), in reply to darksleep
